advances: A full-dimensional sharp singleton lift of the concrete twenty-point tetrahedron exists. The construction below has 36 actual lattice points, four singleton parity classes, and reflection maximum three. Its long fibers are at indices 7, 10, 11, and 16. Four elementary affine inequalities certify its complete convex-hull lattice census, and the original sixteen midpoint rows certify every reflected pair. The proof also establishes the proposed necessary reduction to 256 singleton length profiles. The complete new parity/reflection profile and one exact Boolean next lift are supplied. These results resolve existence in this subgoal; they do not provide a sequence with vanishing normalized reflection gain or resolve the locked weak Oertel conjecture.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. Accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7 supplies the complete old lattice census and original midpoint/parity tables. Accepted fact 32c2c11ba617f80f supplies the proved local inequalities and forced-midpoint rule used in the necessary reduction and the sharp upper bound for the constructed lift. All new geometric containments, affine inequalities, lattice-point exclusions, reflection counts, and the next product lift are proved above with exact integer arithmetic and elementary convexity. SageMath 10.8 over \(\mathbb Q\) was used for discovery and an independent finite check; no software infeasibility, optimality declaration, or unstated computation is a premise of this proof.
proof:
First establish the necessary reduction, using the local inequalities already proved in accepted fact 32c2c11ba617f80f. For this reduction let \(X\) be an arbitrary set satisfying its stated hypotheses. Its actual nonempty integer fibers are consecutive intervals \(I_{p_i}=\{a_i,\ldots,a_i+L_i-1\}\). Here \(a_i\) and \(L_i\) are exactly the lower endpoints and fiber lengths denoted \(a_x\) and \(L_x\) in that accepted fact, with \(x=p_i\) and its lift \(A\) replaced by the present \(X\).

For each old parity class \(C\subseteq B_3\), use the same three local counts as in accepted fact 32c2c11ba617f80f. Thus \(q(C)\) is the number of lifted points over \(C\), plus the number of singleton last-coordinate parity refinements of \(C\); \(t(C)\) counts old reflection-three points of \(C\) whose actual fibers have length two; and \(f(C)\) counts old distinct endpoint pairs in \(C\) producing two integer last-coordinate midpoint heights. The accepted proof establishes \(\sum_C f(C)\le\sum_C t(C)\), and the local bounds \(2q(C)+t(C)-f(C)\le9\) for size-two classes and \(2q(C)+t(C)-f(C)\le11\) for size-three classes. There are four classes of each size, by accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7. Therefore sharpness gives

\[
80=2\bigl(|X|+s(X)\bigr)
\le 2\sum_Cq(C)+\sum_C\bigl(t(C)-f(C)\bigr)
\le 4\cdot9+4\cdot11=80.
\]

It follows that every local inequality is an equality and \(\sum_C(t(C)-f(C))=0\). Reading equality from the proved exhaustive local table gives precisely the following possibilities. For a size-two class the length multiset is \((1,2)\), \((1,3)\), \((1,4)\), or \((2,2)\). In the middle two cases \(t-f=-1\); in the first and last cases \(t-f=1\). The \((1,3)\) case must have \(q=5\) and \(f=1\), which means the singleton and the lower endpoint of the length-three fiber have the same last-coordinate parity.

For a size-three class the length multiset is \((1,1,2)\), \((1,2,2)\), or \((2,2,2)\). In the first case the length-two fiber is at an old reflection-three point, and \(q=5,t=1,f=0\). In the second case both length-two fibers are at old reflection-three points, and \(q=5,t=2,f=1\). In the third case \(q=6,t=2,f=3\). These are all equality cases: the accepted table has strict upper bound below eleven for every other size-three length multiset, and strict upper bound below nine for \((1,1)\) in a size-two class. Within the \((1,1,2)\) case the two singleton lower endpoints must have the same last-coordinate parity, because this is exactly when the four lifted points split as \((3,1)\), giving \(q=5\).

Let \(a\) be the number of size-two old classes containing a length-three or length-four fiber, and let \(w\) be the number of size-three old classes with all three fibers of length two. The preceding exact values imply

\(0=\sum_C(t(C)-f(C))=(4-2a)+(4-2w)\), so \(a+w=4\).

The accepted midpoint rule says that a pair counted by \(f\) forces an actual two-point fiber at its old midpoint. An all-length-two size-three class has three such pairs. Its two midpoints lying in size-two old classes are as follows; every entry follows from the original midpoint table in accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7.

| All-length-two old class | Midpoints forced in size-two old classes |
| --- | --- |
| \(\{p_0,p_{12},p_{18}\}\) | \(p_{14}\in\{p_{11},p_{14}\}\), \(p_{16}\in\{p_6,p_{16}\}\) |
| \(\{p_2,p_5,p_8\}\) | \(p_6\in\{p_6,p_{16}\}\), \(p_7\in\{p_3,p_7\}\) |
| \(\{p_1,p_4,p_{15}\}\) | \(p_3\in\{p_3,p_7\}\), \(p_{10}\in\{p_{10},p_{17}\}\) |
| \(\{p_9,p_{13},p_{19}\}\) | \(p_{17}\in\{p_{10},p_{17}\}\), \(p_{11}\in\{p_{11},p_{14}\}\) |

A size-two old class forced to contain a length-two fiber cannot contain a length-three or length-four fiber: two nonsingleton fibers in one old parity class must both have length two, as accepted fact 32c2c11ba617f80f proves. Regard the four rows of the displayed table as consecutive vertices of a cycle of length four. Each old size-two class is the edge incident to the two rows that mention it. A nonempty proper set of \(w\) vertices touches at least \(w+1\) edges: one vertex touches two edges; two adjacent vertices touch three and two opposite vertices touch four; three vertices touch four. But the number of old size-two classes without a long fiber is \(4-a=w\). Thus \(1\le w\le3\) is impossible.

If \(w=4\), every point of every old size-two class is forced to have a length-two fiber by the displayed table. All twenty fibers would have length two, and each old class would split into two new classes of its old cardinality. There would be no singleton class, contrary to \(s(X)>0\). Hence \(w=0\) and \(a=4\): every old size-two class has one long fiber and one singleton.

An old size-three class now cannot have lengths \((1,2,2)\). Its two length-two fibers would be at its two old reflection-three points, and their pair would force a length-two fiber at their midpoint. In the four classes in the displayed order, those midpoint indices are respectively \(16,7,10,11\). All lie in size-two old classes, whose lengths are now one and either three or four. This is a contradiction. Consequently every old size-three class has lengths \((1,1,2)\). The four old size-two pairs have \(f=1\), and their distinct midpoint indices are \(5,12,15,13\), respectively for \(\{p_3,p_7\}\), \(\{p_6,p_{16}\}\), \(\{p_{10},p_{17}\}\), and \(\{p_{11},p_{14}\}\). They force precisely the asserted four length-two fibers, one in each size-three class. This proves the necessary 256-profile reduction without bounding any lower endpoint. Each size-three class supplies one singleton refinement. A size-two class with lengths \((1,3)\) supplies one singleton refinement, while one with lengths \((1,4)\) supplies none. Counting the twelve length-one fibers, four length-two fibers, and four long fibers now gives \(|X|=36-k\) and \(s(X)=4+k\), as asserted.

We next verify the concrete construction. The four bottom generators of \(Q\) span a three-dimensional tetrahedron in \(t=0\), since the determinant of the three nonzero old vertex vectors is 78. Any top generator has last coordinate three, so \(Q\) is four-dimensional. The top base points belong to \(P\), and all four vertices of \(P\) occur among the bottom generators. Thus the projection of \(Q\) is exactly \(P\), and \(P\times\{0\}\subseteq Q\). All generators are lattice points, so \(Q=\operatorname{conv}(Q\cap\mathbb Z^4)=\operatorname{conv}(A)\).

To certify that no extra integer height appears, define the following four affine functions of the old base coordinates:

\[
\begin{aligned}
g_1(x,y,z)&=28x-11z,&g_2(x,y,z)&=z,\\
g_3(x,y,z)&=10x+28y-23z,&g_4(x,y,z)&=28-28x-18y+23z.
\end{aligned}
\]

Every point \((x,y,z,t)\in Q\) satisfies \(t\ge0\) and \(7t\le3g_b(x,y,z)\) for each \(b\in\{1,2,3,4\}\). It suffices to check these affine inequalities on the eight defining generators. At each bottom generator all four \(g_b\) are nonnegative, and at each top generator all four are at least seven. These assertions, and every fiber upper bound, can be checked directly in the following complete integer table. The old coordinates are precisely the census of accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7. The last column is \(\lfloor3\min_{1\le b\le4}g_b(p_i)/7\rfloor\).

| \(i\) | \(p_i\) | \(g_1(p_i)\) | \(g_2(p_i)\) | \(g_3(p_i)\) | \(g_4(p_i)\) | Integer upper bound for \(t\) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | \((0,0,0)\) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 28 | 0 |
| 1 | \((1,0,0)\) | 28 | 0 | 10 | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | \((0,1,0)\) | 0 | 0 | 28 | 10 | 0 |

| 5 | \((2,3,4)\) | 12 | 4 | 12 | 10 | 1 |

| 8 | \((4,7,10)\) | 2 | 10 | 6 | 20 | 0 |
| 9 | \((7,11,16)\) | 20 | 16 | 10 | 2 | 0 |
| 10 | \((7,12,17)\) | 9 | 17 | 15 | 7 | 3 |
| 11 | \((8,13,19)\) | 15 | 19 | 7 | 7 | 3 |
| 12 | \((8,14,20)\) | 4 | 20 | 12 | 12 | 1 |

The projection property and the accepted complete old census show that every lattice point of \(Q\) has base one of these twenty \(p_i\). The affine inequalities and \(t\ge0\) bound its integer height by the displayed last column. These are necessary inequalities for \(Q\); no assertion that the four inequalities form its complete facet description is needed.

Every integer height remaining in the table actually occurs. Height zero occurs at all twenty base points because \(P\times\{0\}\subseteq Q\). At each of \(p_7,p_{10},p_{11},p_{16}\), the vertical segment from height zero to its defining top generator at height three lies in \(Q\), supplying heights one and two. Finally the four exact old midpoint identities are

\[
2p_5=p_3+p_7,\qquad
2p_{12}=p_6+p_{16},\qquad
2p_{13}=p_{11}+p_{14},\qquad
2p_{15}=p_{10}+p_{17}.
\]

For each pair, take height two at its long-fiber base and height zero at its other base. The lifted midpoint lies in \(Q\) and has height one, supplying \((p_5,1),(p_{12},1),(p_{13},1),(p_{15},1)\). This proves both inclusions in the claimed lattice census. In particular, these are complete actual fibers and \(|A|=12+4\cdot2+4\cdot4=36\).

We now check every reflected pair. Distinct old lattice bases can have an integer midpoint only when their old parity vectors agree. Accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7 lists all sixteen unordered distinct same-parity pairs, each at a different old center. For the present complete fibers their possible integer midpoint heights are exactly as follows.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

To verify the height column and pair multiplicities directly, every row has a length-one endpoint fiber at height zero. Its partner has height range \(\{0\}\), \(\{0,1\}\), or \(\{0,1,2,3\}\). An integer lifted midpoint requires an even partner height. This gives exactly height zero in the first two cases and heights zero and one in the last case. At each listed height there is exactly one unordered endpoint pair from that old row. Distinct rows have different old centers, so they cannot contribute at the same four-dimensional center. These observations account for all pairs with distinct old bases.

The remaining nonzero reflected pairs are vertical. A length-one or length-two fiber has none. A length-four fiber \(\{0,1,2,3\}\) has exactly one unordered vertical pair at height one, with endpoints zero and two, and exactly one at height two, with endpoints one and three. The only rows centered at the long-fiber bases \(p_7,p_{10},p_{11},p_{16}\) have integer midpoint height zero. Their distinct-base pairs therefore never coincide in center with a vertical pair. It follows that every supported center has either one unordered nontrivial reflected pair or none. Each such pair contributes two oriented nonzero displacements, and each supported center contributes its zero displacement.

The four old vertex points at height zero and the four long-fiber tops at height three have no nontrivial pair. Every other point in the established census has exactly one. Thus exactly eight points have reflection count one and 28 have reflection count three. If an integer center outside \(A\) had any reflected endpoints in \(A\), it would lie in \(Q\) by convexity and hence in \(Q\cap\mathbb Z^4=A\), a contradiction. This proves the all-center reflection assertion, including \(\max_jr_A(j)=3\).

For the complete parity/reflection profile, the old three-bit parity classes are the following ones from accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7. In each of the last two columns the triple records, in order, the cardinality of the new parity class, its number of reflection-one points, and its number of reflection-three points. The column parity is the last coordinate modulo two, so these eight rows specify all sixteen ambient classes in \(\mathbb Z^4\).

| Old parity | Old indices | Even last coordinate | Odd last coordinate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 000 | \(0,12,18\) | \((3,1,2)\) | \((1,0,1)\) |

| 101 | \(10,17\) | \((3,0,3)\) | \((2,1,1)\) |
| 110 | \(9,13,19\) | \((3,1,2)\) | \((1,0,1)\) |
| 111 | \(3,7\) | \((3,0,3)\) | \((2,1,1)\) |

Indeed, each old size-three class has lengths \((1,1,2)\), with its old vertex among the singleton fibers. Its even refinement contains that reflection-one vertex and two reflection-three points, and its odd refinement consists of the height-one point of its length-two fiber, which has reflection count three. Each old size-two class has one singleton and one length-four fiber. Its even refinement consists of the singleton at height zero and the long fiber at heights zero and two, all with reflection count three. Its odd refinement consists of the long fiber at heights one and three, with reflection counts three and one respectively. This proves every table entry, \(s(A)=4\), and \(|A|+s(A)=40\). Accepted fact 32c2c11ba617f80f applies to this actual lift over \(B_3\), so the equality is sharp in its stated lift bound.

Finally, the proposed next lift is explicit: \(\operatorname{conv}(A')=Q\times[0,1]\). To see the nontrivial containment, for \(x\in Q\) write \(x\) as a convex combination of points of \(A\), and split each coefficient between last coordinates zero and one with proportions \(1-u,u\), where \(u\in[0,1]\). This represents \((x,u)\) as a convex combination of points of \(A'\). The product hull is full-dimensional and has integer points exactly \(A\times\{0,1\}\). At any supported center an integer displacement in the new coordinate must be zero, since both reflected coordinates lie in \(\{0,1\}\). Its reflection count is therefore exactly that at the corresponding old point of \(A\), and an outside center has count zero by lattice-convexity. Every old parity class is copied once for each new coordinate parity, proving all asserted cardinalities and reflection profiles. In particular, \(|A'|=72\), \(s(A')=8\), and its normalized reflection ratio remains \(4/3\). The new base \(A\) contains singleton parity classes and has the stated different reflection profile, so reapplying the hypotheses of the old singleton-free base theorem to it would require a new argument. No such reapplication is used here.
statement:
For any nonempty finite set \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^m\), use the canonical oriented, zero-inclusive reflection count \(r_X(j)=|\{v\in\mathbb Z^m:j+v,j-v\in X\}|\), for \(j\in\mathbb Z^m\). Let \(s(X)\) count ambient parity classes modulo \(2\mathbb Z^m\) containing exactly one point of \(X\).

Let \(B_3=P\cap\mathbb Z^3\), where \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0,0),(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(31,53,78)\}\). The notation \(B_3\) is exactly that of accepted fact 32c2c11ba617f80f, and denotes the set called \(A\) in accepted fact 768d9712b73c4ab7. Use the exact indices \(p_0,\ldots,p_{19}\) of that accepted census, reproduced in the proof below. Define the lattice polytope

\[
Q=\operatorname{conv}\left(
\{(p_i,0):i\in\{0,1,2,19\}\}
\cup
\{(p_i,3):i\in\{7,10,11,16\}\}
\right)\subseteq\mathbb R^4,
\qquad A=Q\cap\mathbb Z^4.
\]

Then \(Q\) is full-dimensional, \(\operatorname{conv}(A)=Q\), and the projection of \(A\) onto its first three coordinates is exactly \(B_3\). The complete integer fiber of \(A\) at each \(p_i\) is

\[
I_{p_i}:=\{t\in\mathbb Z:(p_i,t)\in A\}
=
\begin{cases}
\{0,1,2,3\},&i\in\{7,10,11,16\},\\
\{0,1\},&i\in\{5,12,13,15\},\\
\{0\},&i\in\{0,1,2,3,4,6,8,9,14,17,18,19\}.
\end{cases}
\]

Consequently \(|A|=36\), \(s(A)=4\), and \(|A|+s(A)=40\), attaining the upper bound in accepted fact 32c2c11ba617f80f with singleton parity classes. There are eight parity classes of size three, four of size two, and four of size one. Exactly eight supported centers have reflection count one: \((p_i,0)\) for \(i\in\{0,1,2,19\}\), and \((p_i,3)\) for \(i\in\{7,10,11,16\}\). Every other point of \(A\) has reflection count three, and every integer center outside \(A\) has reflection count zero. The proof gives the numbers of reflection-one and reflection-three points within each parity class. In particular, all four singleton parity classes consist of reflection-three points.

The necessary length reduction is as follows. Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb Z^4\) be any nonempty finite lattice-convex set projecting exactly onto \(B_3\), with \(\max_j r_X(j)\le3\), \(|X|+s(X)=40\), and \(s(X)>0\). No full-dimensionality or height bound is required for this assertion. Its actual integer fibers have length two at indices \(5,12,13,15\) and length one at every other point of an old size-three parity class. In each of the four old size-two classes \(\{p_3,p_7\}\), \(\{p_6,p_{16}\}\), \(\{p_{10},p_{17}\}\), and \(\{p_{11},p_{14}\}\), one fiber has length three or four and the other has length one. Thus there are at most \(4^4=256\) possible length profiles, before compatibility of heights and convexity is imposed. If \(k\) of the four long fibers have length three, then \(|X|=36-k\) and \(s(X)=4+k\). This is a necessary classification, not a claim that all 256 profiles are realizable.

One concrete next lift is \(A'=A\times\{0,1\}\subseteq\mathbb Z^5\). It is full-dimensional and lattice-convex, has \(|A'|=72\), \(s(A')=8\), and \(\max_j r_{A'}(j)=3\). It has sixteen parity classes of size three, eight of size two, and eight of size one; the reflection profile of each old class is repeated twice. In both dimensions the normalized maximum reflection ratio is \(4/3\): \(3/(36/2^4)=3/(72/2^5)=4/3\).
